title: Glossary and one artwork from 'Criptech and the Art of Access'
introduction: In Week 2 we read the introduction to the special issue 'Criptech and the Art of Access' (Chang and Felt, 2024) together in class. This post is my notebook: three words I did not know, and one artwork from the article.
related_work:
Glossary

1. haptic
Dictionary: 'Of or relating to the sense of touch.' (Wiktionary, https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/haptic)
Word origin: 'Haptic' entered English in 1890. It comes from Greek haptikos, 'able to come into contact with', from the verb haptein, 'to fasten' (Online Etymology Dictionary, https://www.etymonline.com/word/haptic).
In the article: Haptic vests were first made for D/deaf and hard-of-hearing people. At 'crip raves' a haptic disc jockey (DJ) mixes the music through the frequency, location and intensity of vibrations, so people feel the music through the body instead of the ears (Chang and Felt, 2024, p. 129).

2. alt text
Dictionary: 'A text caption, associated with an image or other element, that is rendered if the usual content cannot be rendered.' (Wiktionary, https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/alt_text)
Word origin: 'Alt' is short for 'alternative' (1580s), from Medieval Latin alternativus, from Latin alter, 'the other'. 'Text' (late 14th century) comes from Latin textus, 'thing woven', from texere, 'to weave' (Online Etymology Dictionary). As a web term it is associated with the ALT (alternative) attribute of the image tag in HyperText Markup Language (HTML) version 2.0, defined as 'text to use in place of the referenced image resource' (Berners-Lee and Connolly, 1995).
In the article: Alt text lets people who cannot see a picture 'listen' to it with screen-reader software. In the article, the project Alt Text as Poetry by Bojana Coklyat and Shannon Finnegan turns this description text into poetry (Chang and Felt, 2024, p. 130).

3. audio description
Dictionary: 'An audio track on a video recording, timed to the footage of a film, that typically consists of a narrator describing what is happening in the film.' (Wiktionary, https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/audio_description)
Word origin: 'Audio-' (1890s) comes from Latin audire, 'to hear'. 'Description' (late 14th century) comes from Latin describere, 'to write down', from de, 'down', and scribere, 'to write' (Online Etymology Dictionary). As a practice it grew in the United States in the 1980s: Margaret Pfanstiehl described live theatre performances, and the television station WGBH launched its Descriptive Video Service in 1990 (Wikipedia, 'Audio description').
In the article: Audio description uses a voice to describe the picture, so blind people can understand what is happening in a video. In the article, Darrin Martin adds participatory audio description to video-art archives (Chang and Felt, 2024, p. 129). Alt text turns a picture into sound; audio description turns a video into sound.
results_discussion:
Artwork: Andy Slater, Unseen Sound (2023)

Unseen Sound is a virtual space with no picture. The player holds a game controller and finds the way only by sound; when you meet something, it responds with a sound. It was built in the virtual gallery New Art City with spatial audio, and a screen on the wall shows text descriptions of the sounds for Deaf visitors. Slater is a blind artist, and the work asks why virtual reality leaves blind people out; here sound is the main way to sense the world.
